for the unchanged content pairs. But each key lies in the query's future, so both are blocked by a causal mask. RoPE provides a position-dependent score factor; it does not authorize access to future tokens.
07 / Design an honest search result

Top-1 search returns a passage with cosine 0.97, but its version is obsolete and it says renewal is prohibited for this account type. What should the application do instead of reporting "97% confidence, renewal approved"?

Verify permission, current version, account applicability, and the actual claim. Use metadata filtering and task-specific retrieval/reranking evaluation; provide current applicable evidence to the answering model or state insufficient evidence. Cosine ranks a representation under a metric, not the passage's truth or agreement with a desired outcome. High lexical/semantic overlap can coexist with negation and policy exclusions.

Explain token IDs, lookup rows, position handling, hidden states, pooled text vectors, retrieval, and generation without calling all of them "the embedding." Which implementation topics need separate treatment?

A tokenizer chooses categorical IDs. IDs gather token vectors from a learned table. Position handling adds fixed/learned vectors or rotates queries/keys within attention, depending on architecture. Layers compute context-dependent hidden states. A separate configured encoder may pool or otherwise produce one retrieval vector per text. Compatible query/passage vectors rank passages; selected permitted text becomes context for a generative LLM, which predicts IDs and decodes them to text. Word2Vec, GloVe, contrastive embedding-model training, bi-/cross-encoders, and a .NET semantic-search implementation are outside this chapter.
develops the Transformer architecture.

Use these 21 questions to practice a short answer followed by reasoning, an example, and a limitation. Questions 1-10 focus on token representations; questions 11-21 connect position and attention. Use the linked lessons when you need the full derivation, then explain the computational boundary aloud.
Token representations / Questions 1-10
01 / What does an embedding represent, and what does it not promise?
Explain an embedding to an engineer who has only seen token IDs. Does every coordinate have a semantic label?
An embedding represents an item by an ordered list of numerical coordinates, such as the illustrative token row

. A coordinate is one entry in that list; the whole list is a vector. Dense representations use a relatively compact list of learned values rather than a vocabulary-sized selector with one nonzero entry. "Dense" does not mean every entry must be nonzero.

The numbers become useful through a model's training objective: a task that rewards useful predictions or comparisons. They are not a dictionary of inherent labels such as "renewal," "emotion," and "truth." A token lookup row, a context-dependent hidden state, and a whole-text search vector represent different objects at different stages. Name which one you mean. See
the representation definitions
the boundary between stored rows and contextual states
02 / Why not use token ID arithmetic as a meaning representation?
Would two neighboring vocabulary IDs necessarily represent similar tokens?

No. An ID is a categorical address: it selects a vocabulary entry. Renumbering the vocabulary and moving its table rows consistently would preserve the selected vectors, although the numerical differences between IDs would change. That tells you ID distance is not a meaningful language distance.
In our toy table, ID 0 selects renew and ID 1 selects extend. Their coordinate lists are
; comparison uses those values, not the subtraction
. A learned table lets training change representations without changing token identities. It does not guarantee that every semantically related pair will be close.
Revisit the address-versus-value distinction
03 / What is stored in a token embedding table?
Describe its two dimensions, parameter count, and the meaning of a row.
Let V be the number of vocabulary entries and d the number of coordinates per token vector. The table E has V rows and d columns: shape
. Row r contains the d learned values for vocabulary ID r; columns identify coordinate positions, not tokens. There are
stored numerical parameters.
Our four-token, three-coordinate table has shape

04 / How does an embedding layer turn IDs into vectors?
Trace repeated IDs through the layer. Is the ID multiplied into the retrieved row?
A lookup gathers the row at each address, in input order. In our table, ID 1 selects

The equivalent one-hot selector for ID 1 is
: multiply row 1 by 1, the other rows by 0, and add. That yields exactly row 1, not row 1 times the numerical ID. Implementations normally gather directly rather than building these long selectors.
The full selector multiplication explains the equivalence
05 / Where do token embedding values come from?
Distinguish initialization, learning, and ordinary inference. Explain one numerical update.

A typical LLM starts with initialized token-table parameters and adjusts them during training. A loss is a numerical measure of prediction error; a gradient lists how sensitively that loss changes with each parameter. Backpropagation traces those sensitivities through the prediction computation. A simple gradient-descent update subtracts learning rate times gradient from each old value. Some workflows load previously trained rows or freeze them, so "every embedding is always being updated" is too broad.
our fully derived two-choice predictor

; recomputing gives target probability about 0.549834 and lower loss. The signs come from that objective, not a hand-assigned semantic direction. Ordinary inference reads the saved parameters; it does not train the table each time a user sends a prompt. This predictor illustrates gradient-driven token learning, not a complete sentence-embedding training recipe.
06 / How can the same token acquire different representations in different sentences?
Separate the stored token row from the later contextual state, including the decoder's visibility limit.

The same vocabulary ID retrieves the same token-table row in a given saved model. Later layers calculate a hidden state: an intermediate vector that depends on that row and the context the architecture permits it to use. Thus bank can start with one stored row but acquire different states after finance-related versus river-related preceding text. A tokenizer can sometimes split a word differently; this explanation assumes the bank ID is the same.

A causal decoder can use earlier and current positions, not future text. Saying the bank state already knows a disambiguating word that only appears later would be incorrect for that architecture. Bidirectional encoders permit different visibility. Contextual states are newly computed values, not new sense-specific rows inserted into the vocabulary.
The chapter's toy mixtures show the arithmetic

07 / What does cosine similarity measure, and why use it for search?
Calculate a score and explain why it is neither a probability nor a truth test.

Cosine similarity compares the directions of two nonzero vectors. First multiply matching coordinates and add to obtain the dot product. Then divide by the product of their lengths; a length is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates. For our illustrative renew and extend rows:

Dividing out the lengths removes positive scaling, which is useful when the chosen encoder's relevant signal is directional. The score can rank compatible query and passage vectors. It is not "96% confidence," and aligned vectors do not establish agreement or factual correctness. A zero vector has length zero, making this division undefined. Choose the metric specified for the encoder and evaluate retrieval on the actual task; not every embedding system requires cosine.
08 / How do embeddings participate in retrieval-augmented generation?
Trace both the retrieval path and the text delivered to the answering model.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

means retrieving supporting information and supplying it to a model that generates an answer. Split source documents into manageable chunks, encode each chunk with a configured whole-text encoder, and store its vector alongside its text and metadata. Encode the query compatibly, compare query and chunk vectors, filter for permissions and applicability, and select useful passages.
The answering LLM receives the selected passage

as context; the search vectors are not simply pasted in as its token-table rows. In our retrieval example, a high-scoring renewal passage is only a candidate: version, account applicability, and what the passage actually says still matter. Retrieval can miss evidence, and generation can misuse it. Token lookup learning alone does not establish a high-quality text-search encoder.
Follow the two paths and complete ranking example
09 / What does embedding width control?
Explain its storage tradeoff without confusing width, vocabulary size, or context length.

Width d is the number of coordinates in one vector. Vocabulary size V counts possible token rows; sequence length counts occurrences in an input. These are different quantities. More coordinates provide more representational capacity, but whether that improves a task depends on training and model design, not width alone.
A four-row table with width three stores
numbers. At four bytes per number, that is
bytes for values alone. Doubling width to six stores

bytes. Comparing two vectors also uses more coordinate products. Real storage includes other parameters and overhead. Do not change a deployed encoder's width arbitrarily and expect its existing index to remain compatible.
10 / Are embeddings parameters, activations, or both?
Distinguish stored embedding weights from computed representations.

A typical token embedding table is a trainable weight matrix: its stored coordinates are part of the model's parameters. "Weights" is not restricted to numbers that visibly multiply an input in a layer diagram. Lookup also uses learned parameters.
But not every value called an embedding is itself a stored parameter. A contextual hidden state or a returned sentence vector is a computed output, often called an

: a numerical value produced while processing an input. The parameters determine how it is calculated. A useful interview answer names the object rather than asserting that all embeddings are weights or that embeddings and weights are unrelated.
Learning changes parameters

Position and attention / Questions 11-21
11 / Why does ordinary full self-attention need an order mechanism?
Explain why word order matters and how positions make it available. What changes under a causal mask?

Content-only, unmasked self-attention compares each token's query with every token's key and mixes their values. If you reorder all input rows, those relationships move with the corresponding tokens. The outputs are correspondingly reordered, not necessarily identical arrays. This property is called permutation equivariance: the computation follows a rearrangement rather than assigning original-position meaning to it.

Consequently, those content-only comparisons cannot encode that service precedes client in one sentence but follows it in another. Additive position vectors or relative position mechanisms supply order-dependent information. This is a claim about full content-only attention, not every possible Transformer. A causal mask allows only a prefix, so reordering changes which connections are permitted; it is already order-dependent, though not an absolute-position vector.
The symmetric-mixer calculation
12 / How do positional encoding and positional embeddings differ?
Explain the terminology before describing an implementation.

Positional encoding is the broader idea of making a model's computation depend on where tokens occur. Positional embeddings often means learned vectors retrieved by position index, but terminology varies: the name "Rotary Positional Embeddings" does not imply a learned position-table lookup. State the actual mechanism.
In an additive design, token row
plus illustrative position row

. Both rows must have matching width. Learned positions retrieve their row from a table; fixed sinusoidal positions instead generate a compatible row from the position index. This toy addition row is not claimed to come from the sinusoidal formula. Standard RoPE instead rotates query/key coordinate pairs inside attention. Those operations are not interchangeable additions to the same input row.
the architectural comparison
13 / How would you calculate a fixed sinusoidal position vector?
Give the coordinate pattern, a reproducible example, and its placement.

The convention taught here uses coordinate pairs with different angular rates. A rate tells you how many radians the angle advances per position; a radian measures an arc relative to the circle's radius. For even width d=4 and zero-based pair index i, the rate is

Sine gives the vertical unit-circle coordinate and cosine the horizontal coordinate. Store sine then cosine for each pair, filling coordinates 0 through 3 in order:
The resulting position row is

. The trigonometric values are rounded; no row is learned in this fixed method. Add this row coordinate by coordinate to a width-four token row in the additive architecture. Multiple rates create patterns changing at different scales. Do not claim the short example proves unique positions for arbitrarily large indices or useful unlimited context.
14 / Why keep both sine and cosine in a position pair?
Give a concrete ambiguity that one coordinate alone would lose, then explain the shift relationship.
A unit circle has radius one. At angle 0 its horizontal/vertical coordinates are

A fixed angular shift transforms both coordinates by the same rotation rule at that rate. This gives systematic relationships between position pairs rather than independently assigned random rows. Multiple rates add different repeating scales; the learned network can use their patterns, but that is not a promise of perfect ordering at any length.

15 / How do learned positions differ from fixed sinusoidal positions?
Compare where values come from, training, storage, and untrained positions.

A learned position table has one row per supported position and one column per coordinate. Training adjusts its values through gradients from the model's loss, just as other parameters can be adjusted. The address is a position index, not a vocabulary ID. A fixed sinusoidal row comes from functions of the index and specified rates; the position functions themselves have no learned table parameters.
For four supported positions and width three, a learned table stores

values. Position 4 is outside its zero-based rows 0-3; there is no row to retrieve without a deliberate adaptation. A sinusoidal formula can calculate another index, but calculability does not mean the trained model uses that unfamiliar position well. Both methods still operate within the configured model.
The table, gradient paths, and extension example
make the distinction explicit.
16 / What operation does RoPE perform?
Describe a coordinate pair, angle, and resulting representation without invoking unexplained matrix notation.
Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)

turns two coordinates of a query or key as though turning a point in a plane. Position times the pair's angular rate determines how far it turns. Different pairs can use different rates. The rotation mixes each pair's existing content coordinates; it does not replace them with a standalone position row.
For a clearly nondefault illustration rate pi/4 radians per position, position 2 gives angle
. The formulas are new first coordinate
, where x,y are the old coordinates and theta is the turn angle. With x=1, y=0, cosine=0 and sine=1, they give
the four-coordinate example

17 / Where does standard RoPE enter attention?
Does it directly rotate stored token-table rows or values?

First a layer computes a query, key, and value from each hidden-state row through learned linear projections: multiply coordinates by learned coefficients and add. Queries express what a position is comparing, keys provide comparison candidates, and values supply the information mixed by attention.
The three explicit projection products

Standard RoPE rotates query and key pairs after those projections and before their dot-product comparison. It does not directly rotate the stored token table or the value vector in this convention. The changed scores still change the value mixture and later hidden states, so "RoPE has no effect on token representations" would also be misleading. Specify the layer and operation rather than trusting a loose diagram label.
Follow the original RoPE path diagram
18 / Why can RoPE express relative position?
Explain the shared-shift property and what remains dependent on token content.

Rotating a query at position m and a key at position n changes their dot product according to a rotation difference. With unchanged content pairs and the same pair rate, the positional factor depends on the signed gap

, not separately on both absolute indices. A shared shift of both indices preserves that gap. The complete score still depends on the original query/key content; equal gaps alone do not make arbitrary sentences produce identical attention scores.

The transpose, cancellation, and composition derivation

proves the relative relationship beyond this example. RoPE avoids a learned row for each position and supplies a useful relative mechanism, but attention masks can block either comparison and long-context quality needs separate evidence.
19 / Why is a causal mask not a substitute for a position vector?
Separate what the two mechanisms contribute to an attention calculation.

Position handling changes representations or scores based on location. A causal mask restricts which keys a query is allowed to use during next-token prediction. For zero-based query position 1, keys 0 and 1 are allowed; key 2 is in its future and is excluded before normalizing attention weights. RoPE does not grant access to that future key.
the complete masked example

; the blocked future weight is 0 regardless of its large score. The mask supplies order-dependent connectivity but not an explicit absolute index or sinusoidal coordinate. Both mechanisms can operate together; padding masks address yet another visibility condition.
20 / Does computable RoPE mean unlimited usable context?
Distinguish a mathematical position, supported input length, and tested model quality.

No. A rotation formula may accept another position index while a model or service imposes a finite context window: the number of tokens permitted in a request. Predictions can deteriorate beyond the training range even when the software accepts the input. More retained tokens also increase cache storage and attention work.

Scaling or interpolating positions changes the computation. For example, replacing p by p/2 changes angle p times rate into half that angle: position 2 at rate 1 changes from 2 radians to 1. That alone does not establish useful context extension. Use the checkpoint's supported settings and evaluate representative tasks; some extension methods require additional training. This calculation is not a complete model-specific extension algorithm or a performance benchmark.
context/storage discussion
21 / What must a KV cache preserve when using RoPE?
Explain reuse, original positions, and the double-rotation failure.

A key/value cache stores previously computed keys and values so generation can reuse the prefix rather than recomputing it. In a common implementation, each key is rotated using its original position before caching; its value is stored without that direct RoPE rotation. New queries continue with the correct next position. Other storage layouts are possible, but each comparison must apply the correct positional transform exactly once.
With the separate toy rate pi/4, raw key

The cache lesson also traces the incorrect-index-reset case
16. Numbers become useful through objectives and contracts
Identify. Retrieve. Learn. Locate. Compare.
IDs are addresses; embedding values are trainable parameters.
A prediction objective supplies gradients; training updates shared rows, ordinary inference does not.
Dot products, norms, cosine, and distance measure declared geometry, not truth.
Offsets can be useful empirical hypotheses, never universal semantic equations.
Contextual hidden states differ from table rows; whole-text embeddings require a specified encoder/output procedure.
Sinusoidal and learned position vectors can be added to inputs; standard RoPE rotates query/key pairs instead.
Masking restricts visibility; correct cache positions preserve comparisons during generation.
Calculating another position is not evidence of useful unlimited context.
You can now trace the numerical boundary between a token address and a useful representation, and explain why position belongs to the model's computation rather than the ID. Continue to
From Inputs to Predictions: How Neural Networks Learn
to calculate a whole network's prediction and parameter update, then recognize its operations inside Transformer building blocks.

The vectors and scores are teaching examples, not measured production embeddings or API results. Pooling and positional calculations do not establish retrieval quality or usable context length. Complete embedding-model training, context-extension implementations, and a production semantic-search system require separate treatment and evaluation.

From Inputs to Predictions: How Neural Networks Learn
Calculate a network's prediction, follow the error backward, update every parameter, and recognize the same operations inside a Transformer.
Prerequisite: arithmetic; chapters 01-04 refreshed as needed
Original diagrams + complete training arithmetic

Your support service estimates resolution effort from ticket measurements. You can write rules, but the useful combinations keep changing. How can examples determine the coefficients of a prediction program? What actually changes when that program learns?

A neural network is a program built from numerical operations with adjustable values. In this chapter you will execute a small one by hand. Then you will use that experience to distinguish the jobs of attention, a feed-forward network, residual connections, and normalization inside a language model.

No mathematical background beyond arithmetic is assumed. The notation reminders link to fuller earlier lessons. Work through sections 1-7 in order: they form one prediction-to-update story. Sections 8-12 connect it to Transformers; sections 13-15 consolidate it, including
14 interview questions with explained answers

All features, weights, probabilities, and network widths below are invented teaching values, not measurements from a production service or model. They illustrate calculations, not a validated effort estimator or a benchmark.
1. Examples adjust a function, not the laws of arithmetic

A rule-based estimator might say, "Add extra effort whenever a ticket involves two services." You choose both the rule and its coefficient. A learned estimator instead uses examples of inputs and observed outcomes to adjust coefficients against a declared objective. You still choose the measurements, model structure, training procedure, and evaluation. Learning does not remove engineering judgment.

A neural network composes many such functions, including nonlinear ones. A

Weights are not universally interpretable feature-importance scores. Their effect depends on input units, other weights, activations, and downstream paths. A negative weight can suppress a sum, but that is not a claim that the feature is morally negative or globally unimportant.

Keep this neuron's inputs and weights fixed. Replace b=-0.25 by b=-1.25, then by b=0. What are z and the ReLU output? What if both weights become zero?

3. Nonlinearity makes depth do something different
Why not just stack weighted sums? Consider two scalar affine layers: first

A bend, threshold, or smooth input-dependent gate can do that. This expands what a network can represent; it does not guarantee that training finds a useful solution.

Read the ReLU column as a bent line: flat at zero on the negative side, rising one unit per input unit on the positive side. To see why an affine rule cannot replace it, suppose that rule matched outputs 0 at inputs -1 and 0. Its slope would be

, and 0 again. Thus our earlier logits [ln2,0,0] can come from an ordinary output projection. Softmax gives [0.5,0.25,0.25]. This last projection, if fully trainable including biases, has
chooses the largest probability, here resolved.

draws according to the distribution: imagine a uniform number from 0 inclusive to 1 exclusive. Uniform means equal-length intervals have equal probability. Allocate intervals [0,0.5), [0.5,0.75), [0.75,1) to the three choices: a square bracket includes its endpoint; a round bracket excludes it. Their lengths are 0.5, 0.25, and 0.25, matching the probabilities and avoiding overlapping boundaries. Draw 0.62 is at least 0.5 and below 0.75, so it selects waiting. This is a demonstration of sampling, not a claim that an actual engine uses these exact intervals internally. A probability of 0.5 is neither a guarantee nor an assertion of truth.
For an N-token prefix, the hidden table has N rows and width d. Row-oriented output projection uses

, producing N-by-V logits. Training can compare many valid rows with their next-token targets. Ordinary generation takes the last needed row's distribution, selects one token ID, appends it, and repeats. Decoding the generated ID uses the tokenizer's vocabulary contract, not the hidden vector's coordinate labels.
Training changes stored values; inference changes current state

Ordinary generation inference

An attention key/value cache stores intermediate prefix activations to avoid recomputation. It is not an ordinary weight update. A prompt can change context and outputs profoundly without changing stored model parameters. Some separate adaptation systems do train at deployment time; that is an explicit additional procedure, not what "ordinary inference" means here.
These building blocks do not specify one universal implementation. Layer count, width, bias presence, position mechanism, normalization placement/type, activation, and gated FFN design vary.
develops encoder-decoder distinctions, full multi-head projection algebra, RMSNorm, and modern gated blocks.
Predict / Two axes and two kinds of change

A hypothetical vocabulary has 100 entries and model width 8. A prefix has 6 tokens. What are the output-matrix shape, last-token score count, and all-position logits shape? Does appending a generated token require a new row of model parameters?
. One hidden column maps to 100 scores. Six row-oriented hidden vectors give logits shape
. Appending a token changes sequence length and activations, not the vocabulary-sized parameter matrix. The next step can reuse cached prefix information while using the same parameters.
13. Practice: reconstruct the mechanism without a framework
Predict on paper before opening each solution. Investigate the neuron, verify a complete training step, then distinguish the operations inside a Transformer.
1 / A small neuron investigation

Use inputs [1,2], weights [0.5,-1], and bias 0.5. Calculate z, then ReLU, sigmoid, and tanh outputs. Raise only the bias to 2.5; calculate the three outputs again. Finally set both weights to zero, keeping bias 2.5.

. ReLU gives 0; sigmoid gives 0.268941; tanh gives -0.761594. Raising the bias by 2 raises z by 2 to 1: outputs become 1, 0.731059, and 0.761594. If weights are zero, z=2.5 regardless of the inputs. ReLU gives 2.5. With
A constant input-independent output is not necessarily zero.
2 / Verify one gradient and one simultaneous update

In the main network, check the sign and value of v2's gradient. At the old network, perturb only v2 from -1 to -0.999; compute the changed loss. Then explain why this perturbation check is different from the full training step.
The prediction sensitivity is -2 and h2=1.5, so
to the old prediction 0. Loss becomes

. Dividing loss change -0.00299775 by 0.001 gives -2.99775, close to -3. This changes only one parameter to inspect a local slope. The actual optimizer step changed all nine parameters using their old gradients and then recomputed every dependent activation.
3 / Audit an alleged Transformer explanation

A colleague says: "The FFN compares neighboring token IDs, LayerNorm makes probabilities across the sequence, and residuals concatenate the old and new vectors. All new tokens are generated in parallel, and each user question updates the weights." Repair each claim.

The FFN transforms each position's current representation using shared parameters; attention supplies cross-position mixtures, not comparison of categorical token ID magnitudes. Token-wise LayerNorm normalizes feature coordinates within a row and then applies learned scales/shifts; softmax normalizes vocabulary scores or permitted attention scores into distributions. Residuals add matching coordinates, preserving width; concatenation joins coordinate lists and usually changes width.

Known training positions can be processed together under a causal mask. Ordinary autoregressive inference still chooses the next token before using it to predict a further one. A prompt changes context and activations, not ordinarily the stored weights. The training loop needs an objective, gradients, and an optimizer step. Each repaired claim names the operation rather than attributing understanding to a box.
Use these 14 prompts and explained answers to practice the mechanism, its arithmetic, and its limits. Use the linked lessons for the full derivations, then explain the computational boundary aloud.
01 / What computation defines an artificial neuron?
Name its inputs, parameters, intermediate value, and output.
A basic dense neuron multiplies corresponding numerical inputs by learned weights, adds the products and a bias, then applies an activation function:

, output f(z). With x=[2,1], w=[0.75,-0.5], and b=-0.25, the products are 1.5 and -0.5; their sum plus bias is 0.75. ReLU keeps 0.75. Inputs and computed z/output are activations; weights and bias are parameters. This mathematical unit is not a literal simulation of a biological cell.
Review the labeled computation
02 / How does a bias differ from a weight?
Explain what changes when the input is zero and when one coordinate changes.
A weight scales one input contribution; a bias shifts the pre-activation independently of input values. In

, x=0 gives z=-3, and x=1 gives z=-1. Raising the bias from -3 to -2 adds 1 at both inputs; raising the weight from 2 to 3 adds 0 at x=0 and 1 at x=1. Before activation, a nonzero bias makes this affine rather than strictly linear. In a deeper network a weight's sign or magnitude alone is not a complete feature-importance explanation.
Review the baseline exercise
03 / Why use nonlinear activations in hidden layers?
Show what goes wrong with depth made only of affine transformations.
Composing only affine maps gives another affine map:

. Merely adding depth does not escape that function family. ReLU bends at zero: values at -1, 0, and 1 are 0, 0, and 1. A line through the first two is constant and cannot also match the third. Such a nonlinearity makes a deeper network represent different relationships. It does not guarantee accurate training, and a linear identity output can still be appropriate for regression.
Compare the activation definitions and worked values
04 / Which values are parameters, activations, and hyperparameters?
Classify a hidden width, weight, current hidden value, and learning rate.

Weights and biases are trainable parameters; a hidden output computed for the current input is an activation. Hidden width and learning rate configure architecture or training and are hyperparameters. Our two-input, two-hidden, one-output network stores

parameters. Its hidden activation [1,1.5] is not two extra learned weights; a new input can change it without changing those nine stored numbers. The rate 0.05 controls the optimizer step but is not a weight in the forward function.
Review the three categories
05 / What does a forward pass calculate?
Trace one complete input-to-output calculation and state what it does not do.
It evaluates the current network in dependency order. In our main trace, input [2,1] gives hidden pre-activations
. If target 1 is supplied, squared loss is
. A forward pass alone neither calculates all parameter gradients nor updates parameters. It occurs in both training and ordinary inference.
Review shapes and row conventions
06 / How does backpropagation calculate a weight's gradient?
Give a chain-rule product and a branch-sum example.
Backpropagation works backward through saved operations, multiplying local derivatives along a path and adding contributions where paths meet. Our prediction sensitivity is
. For W11 the path multiplies output weight 1, positive-ReLU slope 1, and input x1=2, giving
. For shared input x1, both hidden routes contribute:
. Omitting the second route would be wrong. The gradient describes local loss sensitivity, not how much a parameter is globally to blame.
07 / What does gradient descent do?
Calculate an update and explain the role of the step size.
It subtracts a positive learning rate times the old-point gradient from each trainable value. With W11=1, gradient -4, and rate 0.05,

. Subtracting a negative number increases the weight because increasing it locally decreases this loss. The rate controls distance, not just direction. For L=(w-1)^2 at w=0, rate 2 sends w to 4 and loss from 1 to 9, so finite steps are not guaranteed improvements.
Review all nine updates and the re-evaluated loss
08 / Why are backpropagation and optimization separate?
Describe the output of each operation and a common implementation mistake.

Backpropagation returns derivatives: in our network the output-weight gradients are [-2,-3] and output-bias gradient is -2. It leaves the stored parameters unchanged. Plain descent then uses rate 0.05 to change output weights [1,-1] to [1.1,-0.85] and bias 0.5 to 0.6, along with the first-layer updates. AdamW would consume gradients using a different stateful rule.

Compute gradients for one consistent forward state before updating; do not backpropagate half the network with newly changed output weights. Also clear stale stored gradients unless accumulation is intentional. Calling loss calculation alone is not either operation.
Review the training-loop pseudocode
09 / What makes a network an MLP?
Distinguish hidden layers, raw inputs, and recurrence.

An MLP is a feed-forward composition of learned layers with hidden nonlinear activations, commonly dense affine transformations. Our main model maps width 2 to hidden width 2 to output width 1; its raw input coordinates are not another learned transformation. Each hidden coordinate uses both inputs, and the scalar output uses both hidden values. A recurrent state from a previous sequence step is not part of this simple feed-forward architecture. Adding a second hidden layer repeats affine transformation plus activation on the first hidden output.
Review the two-matrix FFN form
10 / What job does an MLP-like FFN have in a Transformer?
Explain sharing, expansion, and what it does not mix.

A token-wise FFN transforms each position's representation, often expanding width, applying a nonlinearity, and contracting back. Our width-two example sends [2,1] through [2,1,1] to [3,0], while [1,2] goes through [1,2,-1], then ReLU [1,2,0], to [1,2]. The same matrices serve both positions, so 17 parameters remain 17, not 34. Attention handles cross-position mixtures; this FFN uses context already encoded in each input row. "Independent at each position" does not mean independently learned weights at every position.
11 / What is added by a residual connection?
Calculate its forward value and explain the backward route.
A residual adds a shape-compatible input to a branch output: x+F(x). With x=[2,1] and F(x)=[3,0], output is [5,1], not the concatenated [2,1,3,0]. For scalar F(x)=0.1x, total sensitivity is

. Incoming loss sensitivity 2 therefore gives 2.2, including 2 through the direct path. This can help gradient propagation in deep networks. It does not guarantee preservation or nonzero gradients: F(x)=-x would cancel the input and give derivative 0.
Review the original path diagram
12 / What exactly does token-wise LayerNorm normalize?
Calculate the statistics before explaining its purpose.
It calculates statistics across feature coordinates within one token row. For [1,3], mean is 2; deviations are [-1,1]; variance is
. With epsilon=0.00001, divide by
to get approximately [-0.999995,0.999995]. Learned gamma=[2,0.5] and beta=[0.1,-0.2] then give approximately [-1.899990,0.299998].

Each token uses its own statistics but shares learned feature-wise scales and shifts. It helps control activation scales for optimization, not normalize vocabulary probabilities or prove semantic correctness. Positive epsilon avoids zero division for constant rows. The learned final affine transform need not preserve zero mean/unit variance.
Review the full ledger and constant-row case
13 / What changes during training versus ordinary inference?
Distinguish weights, activations, a prompt, and a key/value cache.

Training runs forward, measures a target-based loss, backpropagates gradients, and uses an optimizer to update parameters. Our complete step changed nine parameters and changed the same input's prediction from 0 to 1.595; its loss fell from 1 to 0.354025. Inference uses stored parameters to compute activations and predictions without that update procedure.

A new prompt or newly generated token changes activations and context. A KV cache retains prefix activations for reuse. Neither is by itself a weight update. Explicit fine-tuning or test-time adaptation is an additional training mechanism, not a consequence of merely asking a question.
Review the two procedures side by side
14 / Why can Transformer training parallelize positions differently from an RNN?
Keep the causal mask and generation dependency in your explanation.

An RNN state depends on the preceding state. Our toy rule required h1=2 before h2=1, and h2 before h3=1.5. Within a Transformer layer, the known input rows can instead have their projections and attention mixtures calculated together, with a causal mask excluding future keys from each row. This permits position-parallel training work; it does not remove dependencies between stacked layers.

Ordinary autoregressive generation still obtains a new token before appending it and predicting the next unknown one. A cache avoids recomputing the prefix; it does not make all future tokens known. Parallelism is an architectural opportunity, not a universal hardware speedup or evidence that attention always learns a correct long-range relationship.
Review the recurrence and masked mixtures
15. Learning is a loop of explicit numerical operations
Compute. Compare. Differentiate. Update.
Weights multiply inputs; biases shift sums; activations change the function family.
A forward pass computes activations using current parameters.
A loss declares a numerical objective; backpropagation calculates its local sensitivities.
An optimizer updates parameters; a fresh forward pass tests the resulting prediction.
A position-wise FFN transforms each token; attention mixes permitted token positions.
Residual addition supplies a direct route; LayerNorm rescales within a token's features.
Output projection creates vocabulary logits, softmax creates probabilities, and selection creates a next token.
Ordinary inference changes current context and activations, not stored weights.
You can now reproduce a complete nine-parameter learning step and identify the mathematical job of each major block in a decoder-only model.

text: Part I / From mathematics to models / 06
Inside the Transformer: How Attention Builds Context
Follow token rows through attention, a complete decoder block, and next-token selection; then recognize which architectural changes affect computation and memory.
Prerequisite: chapters 01-05, refreshed at point of use
Original diagrams + reproducible tensor calculations

A request arrives as text. A response leaves as text. Between them, where does one token acquire information from another, and how do those contextual numbers become the next token? An architecture diagram should answer that question, not replace it with unexplained boxes.

We will calculate a tiny model rather than pretend to inspect a production model's thoughts. Read sections 1-11 in order: they assemble one forward computation. Sections 12-15 explain training, memory and implementation variations. The
section has 20 prompts with explained answers.

Every tokenization, coefficient, width and probability used below is a teaching stipulation, not a measured model output. We distinguish the original encoder-decoder Transformer from an illustrative pre-normalized decoder-only model. No single diagram specifies every Transformer, and a weighted representation is not a verified explanation, fact, or human understanding.
1. A sequence needs relationships, not just isolated features
is an ordered collection, such as token IDs. A

is an intermediate numerical representation. In "The worker retried the job because it failed," context can help distinguish what "it" refers to. That sentence motivates exchanging information; it does not prove that a head reliably resolves pronouns.
A recurrent neural network, or
, carries a state between positions. Recall

, t is the position, x is its scalar input, and h0=0. For inputs [2,0,1], calculate h1=2+0=2, h2=0+0.5(2)=1, and h3=1+0.5(1)=1.5. The third step waits for the second. The first input's contribution reaches h3 as 2(0.5)(0.5)=0.5. Practical RNNs use vectors, learned maps and nonlinearities; LSTM and GRU names denote gated recurrent variants whose full equations are deferred.

provides a different route: a position compares its query with permitted keys and combines the associated value vectors. The projections of known input positions within a layer can be computed together. Layer 2 still waits for layer 1, and ordinary generation still waits for each unknown next token. A shorter dependency path can help with distant relationships; it is not a guarantee of accuracy at every context length.
Architecture names describe information paths. Encoder-decoder cross-attention is absent from our decoder-only trace.

Transformer for tasks such as translation. An encoder builds source-sequence states using self-attention and a feed-forward network. Its decoder has causal target self-attention, cross-attention to those source states, and a feed-forward network. Residual additions and normalization accompany the sublayers. The original six-layer stacks are historical settings, not requirements. "Identical layers" means the same structural pattern, not necessarily tied parameter values.
Three common families, not interchangeable input/output contracts
All nonpadding source positions in ordinary bidirectional self-attention
Classification or trained text representations; BERT
Current and earlier prefix positions under a causal mask
Next-token generation; GPT-style models
Full source states plus a causal target prefix
Conditional sequence generation; T5

means a source position can use earlier and later source positions, not that the model generates text backward. Classification needs an appropriate prediction head; retrieval needs a trained representation/aggregation contract, not arbitrary encoder outputs. Next-token prediction is a broadly usable learning objective, but decoder-only popularity does not make the other families obsolete.
Predict / Two sequences or one?

A translation model has four source tokens and has generated two target tokens. Which sequence supplies a decoder cross-attention query, and which supplies its keys? Does an RNN's fourth toy input x4=0 wait for h3?

The decoder's target state supplies the query; the four encoder source states supply keys and values. Source and target lengths need not match. The recurrence must use h3=1.5, so h4=0+0.5(1.5)=0.75. A causal Transformer can process known target positions together during training, but cannot know a not-yet-selected target token during ordinary generation.
2. Give every axis and operation a meaning
is one number; a vector is an ordered coordinate list; a matrix is a rectangular table. A

generalizes such indexed arrays to more axes. An axis identifies what varies, and its size counts the available entries. Shape [B,N,d] means B examples, N token positions per example, and d feature coordinates per position. It does not mean B multiplied by N is a token ID. We omit the batch axis while calculating one example;

Use token rows throughout this chapter. X has shape N-by-d; Xij is coordinate j of token position i, with i from 1 through N and j from 1 through d. An individual vector is otherwise a column in this book; row multiplication XW uses the transposed weight layout of a column expression Wx. A superscript T means
, swapping rows and columns, not inversion. A matrix product's inner sizes must match.

The capital sigma means sum: multiply matching entries, then add as r runs through all input coordinates. W has d rows and as many columns as the output width. For row [2,1] and output column [3,-1], the entry is 2(3)+1(-1)=6-1=5. Calling this learned map a projection does not imply a perpendicular geometric projection. A
combines weighted input contributions and sends an all-zero input to zero. An
also adds a constant offset, or bias. A nonzero bias makes the map affine, even if a framework calls it linear.
is positive for any finite real z; e is approximately 2.71828. It extends repeated multiplication, with

. The natural logarithm ln(a) reverses exponentiation for positive a: exp(ln3)=3 and ln1=0. A nonnegative square root of a nonnegative a is the nonnegative number whose square is a: square root of 4 is 2 because 2(2)=4. Calculator values below are rounded only when displayed.
gives the fuller function lesson.
Notation ledger for this chapter
Batch examples, sequence positions, model width; positive integers
Vocabulary size and its Vocab-by-d learned embedding table
Query-head count and key/value-head count
Key/query width per head, value width per head, FFN intermediate width
Computed queries, keys and values; V is not vocabulary size
Query position, key position, or coordinate as specified locally; not vocabulary IDs
Predict / Read a shape before multiplying
X is 3-by-2 and W is 2-by-4. What is XW's shape? Can you instead multiply X by a 3-by-4 matrix? What is exp(ln2)+exp(0)?

XW has 3 rows and 4 output coordinates: 3-by-4. The inner sizes 2 and 2 match. A 3-by-4 W would require matching 2 with 3, so that product is invalid. The exponential sum is 2+1=3, not ln2 or 2e. A tensor shape tells you which operations are possible before you inspect its entries.
3. IDs choose rows; position and context change states
A tokenizer turns text into vocabulary IDs using a checkpoint-specific contract. A
is saved model parameters and their configuration. Tokens need not be whole words;

separates characters, bytes, tokens and IDs. For this deliberately invented tokenizer, use vocabulary IDs 0="queue", 1="job", 2="<end>". The text "queue job" becomes [0,1]. These are addresses, not semantic magnitudes.
Worked example / Two lookups and two additions

Choose Vocab=3, d=2. The learned table E has rows [0.8,0], [0,0.8], [0.1,0.1]. IDs 0 and 1 select the first two rows, producing a 2-by-2 table, not the full 3-by-2 vocabulary table. Choose learned position rows P1=[0.2,0] and P2=[0,0.2]. Add matching coordinates:

Token count and width remain 2. If ID 0 occurred at position 2, its input would be [0.8+0,0+0.2]=[0.8,0.2], despite selecting the same learned token row. Training can change E and P; a new request changes selected rows and computed states without ordinarily updating the parameters.
tells the computation about order. Content-only full self-attention is

: rearranging token rows rearranges its outputs correspondingly, rather than producing an identical ordered output. A causal mask already introduces order-dependent connectivity, but is not equivalent to a rich position representation.
demonstrates this distinction. Learned additive positions, sinusoidal additive positions and rotary positions are different mechanisms, not three mandatory simultaneous steps.
, rotary position embeddings, ordinarily rotates coordinate pairs of Q and K rather than adding P to X. Recall

: a quarter-turn sends [a,b] to [-b,a]. For unrotated q=k=[1,0], dot product is 1(1)+0(0)=1. Rotate both by one quarter-turn: [0,1] dot [0,1]=0+1=1. Rotate only the key: [1,0] dot [0,1]=0. The relative rotation changes the comparison; a shared rotation leaves it unchanged. Real RoPE uses specified rates on multiple pairs, with values normally unrotated. Our scalar-head main trace cannot rotate a pair and therefore uses additive positions instead.
Predict / Three different controls
If "job" moves to position 1, what is its additive input? Does moving it change E? Does a quarter-turn authorize access to future tokens?

ID 1 still selects [0,0.8], and P1 adds [0.2,0], giving [0.2,0.8]. The stored E is unchanged. Rotation supplies position-dependent comparisons; it does not decide whether a key is allowed. A separate mask enforces that boundary. Being able to calculate more positions also does not establish reliable quality beyond a model's evaluated context range.
4. Queries compare; values carry the mixture
is a computed comparison vector for the position requesting information. A
is a comparison vector for a candidate position. A

is the vector contributed by that position. The search analogy is useful only for roles: these are numerical projections, not literal search strings, indexed documents or a truth-verification system. Learned weights determine all three.

For one head, WQ and WK have shape d-by-dk and WV d-by-dv. Q and K have N rows of dk coordinates, and V has N rows of dv coordinates. Query and key widths must agree for their dot product; value width can differ. These formulas omit optional biases and any position rotation. In a pre-normalized block, the X entering these formulas is the normalized branch input.
Worked example / Derive head A, not just its result

Take section 3's two rows [1,0] and [0,1], with dk=dv=1. Head A has WQ=[1,1]T, WK=[0,ln3]T and WV=[2,4]T, each shape 2-by-1. First-row products give q1=1(1)+0(1)=1, k1=1(0)+0(ln3)=0 and v1=1(2)+0(4)=2. Second-row products give q2=0(1)+1(1)=1, k2=0(0)+1(ln3)=ln3 and v2=0(2)+1(4)=4.

Thus Q=[1,1]T, K=[0,ln3]T, V=[2,4]T. The parameters are the projection entries; these six outputs are input-dependent activations. The particular ln3 coefficient was chosen to make the later softmax arithmetic exact, not learned from text.
Head A: separate matching information from contributed information
Predict / Reuse the same weights
If the branch input row becomes [1,1], calculate this head's query, key and value. Does it acquire a new projection matrix?

Query is 1(1)+1(1)=2; key is 1(0)+1(ln3)=ln3; value is 1(2)+1(4)=6. The same stored matrices produce new activations. A larger key score is not automatically a larger value: their projections have different jobs and coefficients.
5. Score, scale, mask, normalize, then mix
multiplies corresponding coordinates and adds them;
gives its geometry. QKT has shape N-by-N: row i is query i, column j is key j. A

allows j at most i, including the current position, because that position's state predicts the next token. A padding mask excludes nonexistent input positions; padding and causality solve different problems.

sij is the scaled, masked score for query position i and key position j; r indexes a key/query coordinate; M is the additive mask. In the piecewise definition, use the first case when j is at most i and the second when j is greater. Negative infinity is a mathematical exclusion convention: as a blocked score tends downward without bound, its exponential tends to zero. Implementations may use explicit masking or supported sentinel values. Do not multiply an already computed probability by zero and call that the same normalized operation. Every evaluated row must retain at least one permitted key; all-blocked rows require explicit handling, not division by zero disguised as an answer.
The access table and the weight table are different objects. A permitted key need not receive most of a row's weight.

turns one score row into nonnegative weights summing to one. Exponentiation makes finite scores positive; division by their sum sets the total to one. It compares entries within that row, not all rows together.
describes a distribution over specified alternatives; attention weights are mixture weights over permitted positions, not vocabulary-token probabilities or factual confidence.

aij is the weight assigned by query i to key j; u indexes a candidate key in the normalizing sum; c indexes one value coordinate from 1 through dv. A is the table of aij weights, and O is the output table with N rows and dv columns. Each output coordinate is a weighted sum of the matching value coordinates. Mathematically O=AV. A

means weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so each coordinate lies between the smallest and largest corresponding permitted value coordinates. The full attention map is nevertheless nonlinear in its input because the scores and weights depend on that input.
Worked example / All four scores, then both output rows

Head A's raw score products are q1k1=1(0)=0, q1k2=1(ln3)=ln3, q2k1=1(0)=0 and q2k2=1(ln3)=ln3. With dk=1, the divisor is 1, so scaling changes nothing. The causal mask gives rows [0,-infinity] and [0,ln3].

Row 1 has exponential entries [1,0], sum 1 and weights [1,0]. Its output is 1(2)+0(4)=2. Row 2 has exponentials [1,3], sum 4 and weights [1/4,3/4]. Its output is (1/4)(2)+(3/4)(4)=0.5+3=3.5. Output shape is 2-by-1. Without the mask, row 1 would also give 3.5 and would improperly use the second token while predicting it.
First make the spread calculation visible. A
is the mean of squared differences from that mean;
is its nonnegative square root. For equally likely outcomes [-1,1], mean is (-1+1)/2=0 and variance is (1+1)/2=1.

choices do not influence one another's probabilities. Adding two independent choices from [-1,1] gives four equally likely sums [-2,0,0,2]. Mean is zero; variance is (4+0+0+4)/4=2. Dividing each sum by square root of 2 divides its squared deviation by 2, bringing variance back to 1.

If query/key coordinates are approximately independent, centered (mean zero) and unit-variance, each product has variance about one, and a sum of dk such products has variance about dk. Dividing scores by square root of dk brings that approximate standard deviation back toward one. This is initialization-scale reasoning under stated assumptions, not a guarantee for arbitrary learned vectors.
applies these same statistical operations within a token.
Worked example / A nontrivial divisor

For a separate width-two head, choose q=[2,0], keys [1,1] and [0,1]. Raw scores are 2(1)+0(1)=2 and 2(0)+0(1)=0. Divide by square root of 2, approximately 1.414214: scaled scores are approximately [1.414214,0]. Their exponentials are approximately [4.113250,1], sum 5.113250, giving weights approximately [0.804430,0.195570]. With values [1,2] and [3,0], the first coordinate is 0.804430(1)+0.195570(3), approximately 1.391141; the second is 0.804430(2)+0.195570(0), approximately 1.608859.

Without scaling, scores [2,0] give weights approximately [0.880797,0.119203]. Still larger differences, such as [10,0], give approximately [0.999955,0.000045]. This concentration is called softmax saturation. A
measures local output change per small input change. Holding other scores fixed, a weight a has sensitivity a(1-a) to its own score;
derives this. At a=0.5, calculate 0.5(1-0.5)=0.25; near a=0.999955, calculate 0.999955(0.000045), approximately 0.000045. Scaling helps control this effect; it does not force equal weights.

For numerical stability, subtract a row's largest permitted score before exponentiating. This leaves ratios unchanged because every exponential is divided by the same factor. For [0,ln3], shift by ln3: exponentials become [1/3,1], sum 4/3, and weights remain [(1/3)/(4/3),1/(4/3)]=[1/4,3/4]. Do not exponentiate huge scores unnecessarily.
Predict / A mask is not a position vector

For head A's first row, someone computes unmasked weights [1/4,3/4], then discards the second value and returns 0.5. Repair the result. For row 2, if both keys equal zero but values stay [2,4], what is the output?

Exclude the future key before normalization. The remaining exponential is 1 and denominator is 1, so weight 1 returns 2, not 0.5. Take row x=[1,2]. Stipulate router logits [ln3,ln2,0], whose softmax exponentials [3,2,1] sum to 6, giving [1/2,1/3,1/6]. Choose the two largest, then renormalize their weights: retained sum is 1/2+1/3=5/6; weights are (1/2)/(5/6)=3/5 and (1/3)/(5/6)=2/5.

To expose arithmetic, use simplified affine experts F1(x)=[x1,x2+1] and F2(x)=[2x2,0], rather than pretending to derive full production FFNs. F1([1,2])=[1,3], F2([1,2])=[4,0]. The weighted output is [(3/5)(1)+(2/5)(4),(3/5)(3)+(2/5)(0)]=[0.6+1.6,1.8+0]=[2.2,1.8]. Other routing/weight conventions exist; this exact top-two renormalization is our stipulation.

If each of eight experts hypothetically has 100 stored parameters and two are selected per token, total expert storage is 8(100)=800 parameters, while the selected experts use 2(100)=200 parameter entries for that token. Router, shared components and activation/communication costs are excluded. Sparse expert evaluation can offer more total capacity for a given active compute budget, but uneven routing can overload experts; distributed expert placement can add communication and memory costs. No comparison here predicts a real model's quality or speed.
FlashAttention changes how the same attention is evaluated
is an IO-aware exact attention algorithm, up to floating-point numerical differences.
means moving data between memory levels. A

is a small block of entries processed together. Instead of writing an entire score and weight matrix to larger GPU memory, tiled computation keeps useful working data in faster local storage and accumulates outputs. It does not discard distant keys or change softmax into an approximation. The full set of permitted comparisons still exists.
Worked algorithm bridge / A one-row streaming normalizer

Recover head A's second-row result without keeping both weights. Maintain the largest processed score m, an exponential sum l measured relative to m, and a correspondingly scaled weighted-value sum z. For the first score 0/value 2, m=0, l=exp(0-0)=1, z=1(2)=2.

When score ln3/value 4 arrives, new maximum m'=ln3. Old contributions rescale by exp(m-m')=exp(-ln3)=1/3; the new contribution has exp(ln3-m')=1. Thus l'=(1/3)(1)+1=4/3, and z'=(1/3)(2)+1(4)=2/3+4=14/3. Final output z'/l'=(14/3)/(4/3)=14/4=3.5, exactly the earlier mathematical answer.

This scalar demonstration explains stable accumulation; it is not a production GPU kernel or all FlashAttention scheduling details. For vector values, z stores one accumulated sum per value coordinate. A newly larger maximum rescales every old sum consistently. Real implementations tile multiple queries/keys, handle masks and gradients, and use architecture-specific kernels. Their changed accumulation order can change low-order floating-point bits. Reduced intermediate storage does not erase full-attention's quadratic pair count.

For a new permitted scalar score s and value v, primes mean updated accumulators; alpha rescales old contributions and w is the new exponential contribution. Here m is the running maximum, not the earlier FFN width; l is an exponential sum, not the numeral one. Initialize from the first permitted score s and value v with m=s, l=1, z=v, then apply these rules to later entries. At least one permitted entry is required. Divide z by l at the end. Since exp(s-m') uses a nonpositive argument, this rule avoids unnecessarily huge exponentials.
Predict / Three kinds of efficiency

Does GQA reduce the number of query outputs? Does MoE store only the selected experts? If the two equal FlashAttention bridge scores are 0 and 0 with values 2 and 4, calculate the accumulators and output.

GQA shares KV heads but preserves separate query-head outputs. MoE must store or otherwise make its expert parameters available; selecting a subset reduces per-token expert computation, not automatically total resident storage. After the first score, m=0, l=1, z=2. The second leaves m=0 and adds exponential 1: l=2, z=2+4=6, output 6/2=3. These changes respectively concern KV representation, routed feature computation, and memory-efficient execution of attention; they are not the same optimization.
15. The serving engine executes; the application supplies a contract

Calling a model API delegates numerical execution, not responsibility for the request. The application constructs messages, history, tool results and retrieved context. The serving engine encodes them using the required format, runs the model, manages caches and sampling, and returns generated tokens.
separates role/control tokens from visible prose;
separates retrieval vectors from the actual text supplied to a model.
Application responsibility
Model/serving responsibility
Select authorized evidence and construct messages
Apply tokenizer, template and input/mask conventions
Budget history, retrieved text and output allowance
Execute hidden-state projections, attention and feature transforms
Validate tool actions, enforce permissions, handle cancellation
Manage compatible KV state and next-token selection
Display streaming output and evaluate results
Decode/stream generated token pieces under the response protocol

Hidden states may encode learned role distinctions when the format includes them, but neither attention weights nor control tokens are an authorization mechanism. A retrieved paragraph can contain hostile instructions; it does not become trusted because it was close in embedding space. Preserve boundaries and enforce policy outside the model as needed. A token chunk also need not equal a complete word or a complete validated tool command.
Worked engineering check / Reserve the continuation

For a hypothetical 100-token context allowance, messages/format use 12 tokens, evidence uses 45 and conversation uses 23. Used input is 12+45+23=80; reserving 15 generated tokens totals 95, leaving 5. Another 10-token passage would total 105 and exceed this stipulated allowance. This is an input/output budget example, not a model benchmark or a universal API accounting rule.

Prefill/decode, time to first token, inter-token latency, batching, throughput, quantization and GPU serving require separate implementation lessons. This chapter teaches basic causal cache reuse and payload arithmetic, not complete serving algorithms or measured latency. Adding more blocks likewise adds parameters/compute and optimization demands, not an automatic guarantee of improved quality.
Predict / What must the application still decide?
Can a highly weighted retrieved passage authorize a database write? With the budget above, can you add a ten-token passage while retaining the same output reservation?

No. Attention scores describe numerical mixing, not permission, provenance or reliable truth. Authorization and validation remain explicit system duties. The added passage would bring the reserved total from 95 to 105, above 100; shorten permitted content or change the reservation under the actual model/API contract. Do not silently truncate evidence and claim the same request was processed.

Use these 20 prompts to practice the architecture, calculations, and implementation tradeoffs. Explain the reasoning before memorizing the component names; the answers link back to the worked lessons.
01 / What makes a Transformer a sequence architecture?

It composes attention-based exchange with feature transformations, usually wrapped in normalization and residual additions. Head A's query at position 2 scores keys [0,ln3], normalizes [1,3] to [1/4,3/4], and mixes values [2,4] to 3.5. That calculation makes the state depend on other permitted positions. Unlike a recurrent state chain, known input positions' projections within a layer can run together. Generation and successive layers still have dependencies.
Review the architecture paths
02 / Which components belong to the original model and to a decoder-only model?

The original encoder has self-attention and an FFN; its decoder adds causal target self-attention and source cross-attention before its FFN. Residual/norm operations accompany the sublayers. Our decoder-only program instead uses lookup/position, repeated causal attention plus FFN blocks, final normalization, vocabulary projection and selection. Removing the encoder does not leave an invisible cross-attention source. In our trace, two-by-two hidden rows become two-by-three logits, not three new token rows.
03 / Why did attention help replace recurrence in many language workloads?

Known position projections and comparisons can be batched within a layer, and attention provides direct paths between permitted distant positions rather than repeatedly passing through intervening recurrent states. In h_t=x_t+0.5h_(t-1), inputs [2,0,1] require states 2, then 1, then 1.5 in order; the earliest contribution is repeatedly scaled. That toy fading path illustrates a dependency, not a proof that every RNN fails. Accelerator-friendly matrix operations helped scaling, while long-context attention has its own quadratic comparison cost. Neither model quality nor sequential-generation removal follows automatically.
Review the dependency calculation
04 / How do the three architecture families differ?

An encoder-only model usually builds states from full nonpadding input context; a task head can use them for classification or trained representations. A decoder-only model causally predicts a continuation. An encoder-decoder conditions a causal target decoder on separate encoded source states. For four source positions and two target positions, cross scores can be 2-by-4 while target self-scores are 2-by-2. BERT, GPT-style and T5 are illustrative families, not a guarantee of every vendor's hidden implementation.
05 / What is repeated when a model stacks Transformer blocks?

A structural unit transforms incoming hidden states through attention and FFN branches with residuals and normalization. In our Pre-Norm trace, R=X+A(LN1(X)), then Y=R+FFN(LN2(R)). The first row moves [1,0] to [4,1], then approximately [6,2]; model width stays two. A second block receives Y, not the original token lookup again. Repeated structural pattern does not mean all blocks share weights. Norm placement and branch variants must be specified.
Review all intermediate values
06 / How does self-attention make one position contextual?

Q, K and V come from the same sequence's current states. Query/key dot products are scaled, masked and row-normalized; weights combine value coordinates. With q=1, keys [0,ln3] and values [2,4], permitted scores exponentiate to [1,3], sum 4, weights [1/4,3/4] and output 0.5+3=3.5. It is not direct multiplication of token IDs or a dictionary sense lookup. Those weights are input-dependent numerical routing, not a verified explanation of truth.
07 / What changes in cross-attention?

The query comes from the target state table, keys/values from another source table. Shared key/query coordinate width allows comparison even when sequence lengths differ. Our one target query against three source keys produces scores [0,ln2,ln2], weights [1/5,2/5,2/5], and values [2,0], [0,3], [2,3] mix to [1.2,2.4]. Target self-attention remains separately causal; source cross-attention can use the full available source with padding excluded. Injecting a document into one decoder prefix does not by itself create a cross-attention module.
Review both source contracts
08 / What do several heads add, and how are they combined?

Separate learned projections permit different comparisons and value mixtures. At our second position A returns 3.5 and B returns 4; concatenate to [3.5,4], then multiply WO to obtain [3.5+4,3.5-4]=[7.5,-0.5]. Concatenation is not averaging or addition, and head outputs do not run through each other. Multiple heads increase representational options without assigning guaranteed semantic roles. If Hq=2 and dv=1, joined width is 2; WO maps that width back to d.
09 / Why scale the query-key dot product?

With approximately independent centered unit-variance coordinates, the sum of dk query-key products has variance about dk and standard deviation about its square root. Dividing by that square root controls typical initialization score scale. For dk=2, a raw score 2 becomes approximately 1.414214; against score zero its softmax weight is approximately 0.804430 rather than 0.880797. Large score differences can saturate weights and reduce local derivatives. This is assumption-dependent scale reasoning, not a bound on all trained scores or a command to divide by model width.
Review assumptions and arithmetic
10 / What exactly does a causal mask prevent?

Query row i cannot use keys at positions j greater than i. It may use its own token because that row predicts token i+1. In [queue,job], row 1's target is job, so its weights must be [1,0]; head A returns 2 instead of the unmasked 3.5. Mask before normalization; dropping an old weighted term gives the wrong denominator. A position vector or query/key rotation does not enforce this access rule, and a padding mask has a different purpose.
11 / How do residual connections help, and what do they not guarantee?

They add a matching-width input directly to a transformed branch. [1,0]+[3,1]=[4,1] preserves width, not a separately stored original row. With scalar branch F(x)=0.1x, output derivative is 1+0.1=1.1; incoming loss sensitivity 2 becomes 2.2 rather than 0.2 through the branch alone. This direct gradient route can aid optimization. F(x)=-x cancels the result and derivative, so neither information preservation nor successful training is guaranteed.
Review the skip arrows and shape condition
12 / What does LayerNorm normalize?

For each token separately, it subtracts the mean across feature coordinates, divides by square root of variance plus positive epsilon, then applies learned feature scales/shifts. Row [1,3] has mean 2, deviations [-1,1] and variance 1; unit-scale zero-shift output is approximately [-0.999995,0.999995] at epsilon 0.00001. Another token has its own statistics. This controls activation statistics rather than creating probabilities or averaging the sequence. RMSNorm instead divides by a root mean square without centering; the same row becomes approximately [0.447213,1.341639].
13 / Why is Pre-Norm different from Post-Norm?

Pre-Norm computes x+F(LN(x)); Post-Norm computes LN(x+F(x)). The first preserves an unnormalized skip route around the normalized branch, while the second normalizes the sum. With x=[1,3] and constant F=[1,0], Pre gives [2,3]; Post centers/rescales [2,3] to approximately [-0.999980,0.999980]. These numbers demonstrate noninterchangeable order. Many deep modern designs use Pre-Norm for optimization behavior, but it is not a universal specification or a stability guarantee.
Review the exact convention
14 / What does an FFN do that attention does not?

The position-wise FFN transforms the current row's features through learned maps and nonlinearities. Our [1,-1] expands to [1,-1,2], ReLU gives [1,0,2], and contraction produces [2,1]. It does not directly compare neighboring token rows. Attention mixes positions, but is itself also a nonlinear input-dependent operation; saying it is only a fixed average would be misleading. A common FFN expands features then returns to model width for the residual, with shared parameters across positions. GELU or gated variants are architecture choices.
Review feature and gate calculations
15 / Why does the model need a language-model head?

Hidden feature coordinates are not vocabulary scores. A Vocab-by-d matrix U maps a row h to hUT, producing Vocab logits. In our width-two example h=[u,-u] and output rows [ln2,0], [0,0], [0,ln2] give [u ln2,0,-u ln2], three candidate scores. Tied embeddings can reuse an input matrix but are not mandatory. The head changes feature width, not sequence length, and softmax/selection remain separate operations.
Review the complete final projection
16 / What distinguishes a logit from a probability?

A logit is an unnormalized real score, which can be negative and need not sum to anything. Softmax of [ln2,0,0] exponentiates to [2,1,1], sum 4, and divides to [0.5,0.25,0.25]. Adding the same score offset leaves the distribution unchanged because it multiplies every exponential by one common factor. A normalized prediction distribution is not a claim that generated content is true. Attention softmax distributes weights over positions; a language head's softmax distributes probability over vocabulary IDs.
17 / How does grouped-query attention reduce cache payload?

Several distinct query heads reuse a KV head. At fixed B,L,N,dk,dv and stored precision, cache payload follows Hkv rather than Hq. Our four-query MHA example needs 192 bytes; two-KV GQA needs 96; one-KV MQA needs 48. Shared keys [0,ln3] with values [2,4] still give q=1 output 3.5 and q=-1 output 2.5, so sharing does not force identical queries or answers. Payload reduction is not a measured speed/quality guarantee or a runtime replacement for training-compatible projections.
18 / What is sparse about a mixture of experts?

A router chooses a subset of expert feature-transform networks per token. Our router probabilities [1/2,1/3,1/6] select the first two; renormalizing gives [3/5,2/5]. Their outputs [1,3] and [4,0] combine to [2.2,1.8]. Sparse expert evaluation can increase total parameter capacity relative to active per-token work, but the router and shared attention still run. Unselected experts still require storage/availability, and load balance/communication can be expensive. Actual experts are not necessarily interpretable topic specialists, and shared-expert variants exist.
Review the stipulated router
19 / Is FlashAttention approximate or a different attention architecture?

It is an IO-aware execution algorithm for exact attention in mathematical arithmetic, subject to floating-point differences, not a sparse-key selection architecture. Tiling avoids writing full intermediate score/weight matrices to larger memory. Our streaming row maintains scaled sums: first m=0,l=1,z=2; after score ln3/value 4, m=ln3,l=4/3,z=14/3, so z/l=3.5 matches ordinary softmax attention. Full permitted comparison count remains; memory traffic and intermediate storage are the target.
20 / Why does ordinary autoregressive generation remain sequential?

The selected next token becomes context for the following prediction. With prefix [queue,job], our model selects queue, then the next pass receives [queue,job,queue]; it could not know that third ID before selection. Training can batch known shifted targets under a causal mask, and cache reuse avoids recomputing valid old keys/values, but neither supplies unknown future tokens. Execution can parallelize heads, coordinates and independent requests; that is different from removing this within-sequence dependency. Detailed alternative decoding engines are deferred.
Review the axes of dependency
17. Reconstruct the flow, then identify the tradeoff
IDs address learned rows. Position mechanisms and context-dependent computation change states, not dictionary meanings.
Queries and keys calculate permitted weights; values supply the coordinates mixed. Heads have separate projections and a combined output map.
Residuals add matching shapes; normalization compares features; FFNs transform each current row. Their order and variants matter.
The language head makes vocabulary scores. A prediction target drives training; selecting and appending a token drives ordinary generation.
GQA changes KV sharing, MoE changes expert activation, and FlashAttention changes memory-efficient evaluation. None is a universal quality or speed guarantee.
Synthesis / Audit a model diagram

A hypothetical model has B=1, N=4, d=8, four query heads, two KV heads, dk=dv=2 and vocabulary size 10. Give the score shape and entry count; give all-position logits shape. If N doubles, which count quadruples? Why does adding more blocks not prove quality improves?

There are four query heads despite only two KV heads, so score shape is [1,4,4,4], with 1(4)(4)(4)=64 entries in a full square. Logits are [1,4,10], 40 scores. At N=8, full scores are [1,4,8,8], 256 entries, four times 64; logits are 80, twice 40. Cache payload likewise doubles if other axes remain fixed. More blocks increase transformation depth, parameter storage and work; optimization, data quality and evaluation determine whether that capacity helps. A box count is not an accuracy metric.

You can now walk from a token ID to the next generated ID, calculate the key transitions, and challenge a diagram that silently swaps axes or architectures. Detailed Transformer training, production inference and GPU implementations remain future subjects, not chapters already available in this edition.

The complete forward pass and cache/router/tiled-normalizer calculations are teaching examples, not trained model outputs or production kernels. Normalization placement, parameter sharing, and execution details vary by architecture. Full Transformer training, quantization, and production serving are outside this chapter.
