text: Part I / From mathematics to models / 07
Attention in Action: How Models Select and Combine Context
Calculate every query's mixture, follow its gradients, and distinguish changes to information access from changes to cache storage and execution.
Prerequisite: chapters 01-06, refreshed at point of use
Original diagrams + explained numerical experiments

You inspect an attention implementation. It produces the expected tensor shape, but does it mix the right positions, use the right denominator, and reuse only valid cached states? A plausible-looking matrix is not enough. We will make the computation small enough to audit by hand.

assembled a complete decoder forward pass. Here we open the attention operation itself. Sections 1-7 establish its numerical and differentiation contracts; sections 8-12 compare access, caching and execution; section 13 turns the arithmetic into C#. The
section has ten prompts with fully explained answers.
Toy numbers, explicit contracts

All vectors, weights, widths and memory budgets here are stipulated teaching inputs, not observations of a trained model. We omit dropout, a training-time random omission/rescaling mechanism, and biases, constant offsets, unless explicitly introduced. Their detailed implementations are not needed for this arithmetic. Exact identities describe real-number arithmetic; decimals and floating-point code are approximations. No head is assigned a guaranteed grammatical role, and no calculated payload ratio is a measured speedup.
1. Separate matching information from contributed information
Suppose a code assistant sees "The worker released the lease after it expired." Useful context may relate "it" to the lease rather than the worker. This motivates
contextual representations
: intermediate numbers that depend on other permitted positions. It does not prove that an attention head resolves this sentence correctly.
supplies matching coordinates for a position gathering information. A
supplies matching coordinates for a candidate position. A

supplies coordinates to combine after matching. Think of a query, searchable metadata and document content, but stop the analogy there: these are learned numerical maps, not literal search strings, stored documents or verified facts.
. A matrix is a table with rows and columns. Its

counts both. A token-state matrix X has N rows, one per position, and d columns, one per feature coordinate. Entries are dimensionless toy features, not meters or token IDs. Individual vectors are columns elsewhere in this book; token tables use rows, so XW uses the transposed weight layout of a column expression Wx. We omit batch and head axes until section 6.

WQ and WK have shape d-by-dk; WV has shape d-by-dv. Q and K therefore have shape N-by-dk, while V is N-by-dv. dk and dv are positive integer widths. Query/key widths must match for comparison; value width need not equal them. The learned matrices are parameters. Q/K/V are input-dependent activations. In a pre-normalized block, X here means the normalized branch input, not necessarily the initial embedding lookup.
Matrix multiplication combines a row with each output column. Multiply corresponding entries and add: row [a,b] times column [c,e] produces ac+be. A
, written T as a superscript, swaps rows and columns; it is not an inverse. A
is this coordinate-by-coordinate multiply-and-sum comparison. Distinct query/key maps mean their score table need not be symmetric or have a constant diagonal.
Matching and contributed content take different paths. Every token produces a query, key and value in self-attention, not just the final token.
A three-position numerical contract

Choose N=3 and d=dk=dv=2. Labels "worker", "lease", "expired" only identify our three invented positions; they are not a real tokenizer or interpretable feature meanings. A square root is the nonnegative number whose square returns its input: square root of 2 is approximately 1.414214. We write sqrt2 as compact prose shorthand for that number. The natural logarithm ln(a), defined for a>0, reverses the exponential exp(z)=e raised to z: exp(ln2)=2 and exp(ln3)=3. e is approximately 2.71828; exp(0)=1. For a negative exponent, exp(-z)=1/exp(z), so exp(-ln3)=1/3.
Read the two functions in opposite directions
Worked example / Derive every projected row

For row 3, Q is [1(sqrt2)+1(0),1(0)+1(sqrt2)]=[sqrt2,sqrt2]. K is [1(ln2)+1(0),1(0)+1(ln3)]=[ln2,ln3]. V is [1(2)+1(0),1(0)+1(4)]=[2,4]. We chose the coefficients to make later scaling and exponentiation easy. This is not a typical learned projection.
Same states, three different roles
Predict / Change states, not the stored maps
Use the same weights on row [2,1]. Calculate its Q/K/V. Would inference normally overwrite the embedding table?

Q=[2sqrt2,sqrt2], because the first coordinate is 2(sqrt2)+1(0) and the second is 2(0)+1(sqrt2). K=[2ln2,ln3], and V=[4,4]. Different activations came from the same matrices. Ordinary inference produces contextual states without an optimizer update to the embedding table; training can change that table through gradients.
2. Calculate all rows, not just one appealing heatmap

The score table has one row per query and one column per key. In self-attention both counts are N, so QKT is N-by-N: N-by-dk times dk-by-N. Scaling divides each dot product by square root of dk. For this first calculation all three keys are permitted. We will separately impose causality.

i indexes query positions 1 through N; j indexes key positions 1 through N; r indexes matching coordinates 1 through dk. Sigma means sum over r. sij is a scalar score, not a probability. Here dk=2. For query 1/key 1, [sqrt2(ln2)+0(0)]/sqrt2=ln2: the nonzero scale cancels exactly.
Worked example / All nine dot products
Query 1 compares with keys 1, 2, 3: raw products are sqrt2(ln2)+0(0)=sqrt2 ln2; sqrt2(0)+0(ln3)=0; sqrt2(ln2)+0(ln3)=sqrt2 ln2. Divide by sqrt2 to get [ln2,0,ln2].
Query 2 gives 0(ln2)+sqrt2(0)=0; 0(0)+sqrt2(ln3)=sqrt2 ln3; 0(ln2)+sqrt2(ln3)=sqrt2 ln3. Scaling gives [0,ln3,ln3].

Query 3 gives sqrt2(ln2)+sqrt2(0)=sqrt2 ln2; sqrt2(0)+sqrt2(ln3)=sqrt2 ln3; sqrt2(ln2)+sqrt2(ln3)=sqrt2(ln2+ln3). Scaling gives [ln2,ln3,ln6]. Why ln6? Exponentiating a sum multiplies exponentials: exp(ln2+ln3)=2(3)=6, so that sum is ln6.

exponentiates each permitted score, then divides each exponential by their sum. Exponentials are positive for finite real scores, making positive weights; dividing sets their total to one. It is a row operation, not a single denominator for the entire matrix.

u indexes keys in query i's denominator. aij is its mixture weight; A is the matrix of these weights. c indexes value coordinates 1 through dv. O is the N-by-dv output, also written AV. Under masking, sums run only over permitted keys. Attention weights describe mixtures over positions, not vocabulary-token probabilities or factual confidence.
Independent normalizers for the three scaled rows
Worked example / Every output coordinate

has nonnegative weights totaling one. Consequently each output coordinate lies between the smallest and largest permitted value in that coordinate: our first coordinates stay between 0 and 2; second coordinates between 0 and 4. This bounds a head's mixture, not the later learned output projection, residual sum or vocabulary scores. Input-dependent weights also make the complete attention function nonlinear, not a fixed linear average.
Predict / Test a denominator and a coordinate
For query 2, someone divides by 23, the sum of all nine exponentials. Repair it. If V2 becomes [0,7], holding Q/K fixed, what is O2?

The denominator is query 2's own sum 1+3+3=7, so its weights stay [1/7,3/7,3/7]. With the changed value, coordinate 1 stays 8/7. Coordinate 2 becomes (1/7)(0)+(3/7)(7)+(3/7)(4)=0+3+12/7=33/7, approximately 4.714286. Matching scores did not change, but the contributed payload did. The coordinate stays within the new permitted range 0 to 7.
3. Scaling controls a distribution, not a maximum allowed score
Why divide by square root of key width rather than key width itself? The motivation concerns statistical spread under assumptions, not a bound on trained scores. Refresh
: a mean is sum divided by count; a deviation is an outcome minus the mean; variance is the mean squared deviation; standard deviation is its nonnegative square root.
Two independent signs make the spread visible

means choosing one sign does not change the other sign's probabilities. Each sign is equally likely to be -1 or 1, with mean (-1+1)/2=0 and variance (1+1)/2=1. Their four equally likely sums have mean (-2+0+0+2)/4=0 and variance (4+0+0+4)/4=2. Divide each sum by sqrt2: every squared deviation is divided by 2, so variance becomes 2/2=1. Divide instead by 2: variance becomes 2/4=1/2.

For independent equally likely sign-valued query/key coordinates, the four possible products are [1,-1,-1,1]. Their mean is (1-1-1+1)/4=0 and variance is (1+1+1+1)/4=1. Adding independent coordinate products therefore has the same spread pattern illustrated above. More generally, if query and key coordinates are approximately independent across coordinates and from each other, centered and unit-variance, their products have variance about one and a sum of dk products has variance about dk. Its standard deviation is therefore about sqrt(dk). Scaling by sqrt(dk) brings that spread back near one. Learned correlations, different input scales or trained projections can violate those assumptions. Scaling does not guarantee bounded scores or equal weights.
Worked comparison / Do not confuse scaling with masking

Use a separate head with dk=4, query [2,0,0,0], keys [1,0,0,0] and [0,0,0,0], and scalar values 2 and 6. Raw scores are 2(1)+0+0+0=2 and 0. Without scaling, exponentials are approximately [7.389056,1], denominator 8.389056, weights [0.880797,0.119203]. The first value contribution is 0.880797(2), approximately 1.761594. The second is 0.119203(6), approximately 0.715218. Add them: 1.761594 + 0.715218, approximately 2.476812.

sqrt4=2, so scaled scores are [1,0]. Exponentials are [2.718282,1], sum 3.718282, weights approximately [0.731059,0.268941]. Contributions are 0.731059(2), approximately 1.462118, and 0.268941(6), approximately 1.613648. Their sum is approximately 3.075766. Both keys remain allowed. The divisor changed the distribution; it did not delete information access or reduce the output width.
Subtracting a maximum preserves the answer
Large exponentials can overflow a finite computer number.

means evaluating an equivalent expression without unnecessarily producing problematic intermediate values. Subtract a row's maximum m from every permitted score. Since exp(s-m)=exp(s)/exp(m), all numerator and denominator terms share the same divisor and the weights stay unchanged.
Worked example / Stable arithmetic with a large common offset

For scores [1000,1000+ln3], do not calculate exp(1000). Subtract m=1000+ln3, giving [-ln3,0]. Exponentials are [1/3,1], sum 4/3. Weights are [(1/3)/(4/3),1/(4/3)]=[1/4,3/4]. With values 2 and 4, output is 0.5+3=3.5. This is exactly the mathematical distribution of [0,ln3] as well.

In finite floating-point arithmetic, a very negative shifted score can underflow to zero. That may be acceptable within an explicit precision tolerance, but it is not an exact real-number zero or a substitute for the logical mask. Reject unsupported nonfinite inputs instead of returning a success-shaped result.

Merge under a common maximum

The second tile has score t=ln6 and value v=[2,4]. Set the updated maximum m'=max(m,t)=ln6. Old exponentials were measured relative to ln3, so rescale them by alpha=exp(m-m')=exp(ln3-ln6)=1/2. The new contribution has weight u=exp(t-m')=1. Primes here mean updated values, not derivatives.
Worked example / Finish both coordinates

l'=(1/2)(5/3)+1=5/6+6/6=11/6. First numerator coordinate: (1/2)(4/3)+1(2)=2/3+2=8/3. Second: (1/2)(4)+1(4)=2+4=6. Divide: o1=(8/3)/(11/6)=(8/3)(6/11)=16/11; o2=6/(11/6)=6(6/11)=36/11. This is exactly the full-row answer, without storing its three final weights.

For a general new tile, first compute its own maximum mt, denominator lt and vector numerator zt. Set m'=max(m,mt); multiply old sums by exp(m-m') and tile sums by exp(mt-m'), then add. This follows directly because both sums must use the same reference maximum. Initialize from the first nonempty permitted tile; skip fully blocked tiles. Changing tile order need not change the real-number result, but floating-point addition is not perfectly associative.

Full attention still evaluates its permitted query-key comparisons: tiling does not remove quadratic full-prefill arithmetic. 01 / When does attention connect two sequences rather than contextualize one?

Self-attention projects Q/K/V from one sequence's states. Cross-attention projects queries from a target sequence and K/V from a separate source. If there are two target and three source positions, the score table is 2-by-3, output still has two rows. Our first target normalizes [2,1,2] by 5 and mixes [2,0],[0,4],[2,4] to [8/5,12/5]. Available source positions do not obey the target's causal position numbering; source padding and target self-causality are separate restrictions. Adding retrieved text to one decoder prefix is not an architectural cross-attention module.

02 / What parallelism does attention enable, and what remains dependent?

Known positions can be projected and compared together within a layer, and permitted distant positions have direct attention paths. A recurrence instead uses its preceding state: for h_t=x_t+0.5h_(t-1), h0=0 and inputs [2,0,1], h1=2, h2=1, h3=1.5, in that order. Attention's three rows use a single 3-by-3 score operation instead of that recurrent state chain. However layer 2 still needs layer 1, and ordinary token 5 generation needs the selected token 4. Q/K define matching scores; V defines contributed coordinates. Separate learned maps allow the matching and payload representations to differ. 04 / Why scale by square root of key width, and why not call it a guarantee?

Under approximately independent, centered unit-variance coordinate assumptions, adding dk query-key products yields variance about dk. A divisor sqrt(dk) therefore restores variance near one. At dk=4, divide raw scores [2,0] by 2 to get [1,0]. The larger weight changes from about 0.880797 to 0.731059. A saturated weight 0.999 has own-score sensitivity 0.000999, versus 0.25 at weight 0.5; scaling can help avoid excessively concentrated distributions. Trained correlations can violate the assumptions, and value/loss sensitivities also matter. The divisor concerns query/key width, not necessarily model width, and is not a causal mask.
05 / How do MHA, GQA and MQA differ without deleting query heads?

MHA has a KV head per query head; GQA shares each KV head among a specified query group; MQA shares one KV head among all queries. Four-query MHA/GQA/MQA with four/two/one KV heads under our B=1,L=2,S=6,dk=2,dv=3,b=2 assumptions use 480/240/120 payload bytes. GQA queries [1] and [-1] against shared keys [0,ln3] still return 3.5 and 2.5, because their scores differ. Cache storage follows Hkv, outputs and score rows Hq. Compatible projections/group mappings and training are required; changing allocation alone cannot invent a GQA checkpoint or guarantee a quality/speed tradeoff.

07 / What does the KV cache save, and when is reuse valid?

It saves layer-specific computed keys/values for a compatible causal prefix. Old states do not depend on newly appended future tokens, so the new query can reuse them. Appending section 9's K3/V3 gives scores [ln2,ln3,ln6], weights [2/11,3/11,6/11] and output [16/11,36/11], equal to full causal row 3. Each layer has its own cache; old query rows and final response text are not the cached payload. Editing the prefix, changing weights or position conventions can invalidate reuse. 08 / How can FlashAttention avoid full intermediate matrices and still be exact?

Tiled computation keeps stable running maxima, exponential denominators and vector numerators. For scores [ln2,ln3] the first tile has m=ln3,l=5/3,z=[4/3,4]. The ln6 tile raises the maximum, so rescale old sums by 1/2 and add its exponential 1/value [2,4]: l'=11/6,z'=[8/3,6]. Dividing gives [16/11,36/11], the full-row result. Both numerator and denominator must use the same scale. This avoids materializing full weights in large memory; it does not remove permitted pair calculations or sparsify attention. Exact real-number algebra allows low-order floating-point differences, not arbitrary approximation or a universal benchmark claim.
09 / When is attention quadratic, and when is a step linear in context?

Full prefill has N queries comparing with N keys per head: N squared pairs; score/value work grows with their widths. At B=1,Hq=2,N=4,dk=dv=2, the two products use 128 multiplications. N=8 gives 512, four times as many. Causal permitted pairs N(N+1)/2 still grow quadratically; a dense mask need not save allocated squares. One cached decode step has one new query per head against S keys, so work grows linearly in S: with S=4 the same widths use 32 multiplications, and S=8 uses 64. Summing many decode steps again accumulates growing work. Big-O is a growth description, not milliseconds, and KV cache payload is distinct from score intermediates.

10 / Does a high attention weight establish why an answer was produced?

No. It describes one head/query's mixture, not a complete causal explanation of the final output. For weights [0.9,0.1] and scalar values [0,100], contributions are 0.9(0)=0 and 0.1(100)=10: the smaller weight supplies the entire scalar output. Vector directions can also cancel, and output projection, residual paths, FFNs and later layers change how mixed states affect logits. Heads may have overlapping or hard-to-interpret patterns. Attention also cannot retrieve an unseen external paragraph or authorize an action; RAG and permission checks are separate system operations.
